examples: It snowed while I was sleeping.
A burglar broke in while my father was away from home.
My phone rang while I was watching a movie.
I finished making dinner while the children were playing.
An important email arrived during the meeting.
fields.explain:
Adding a clear time marker makes the sentence tighter: その間に／この間に（during that time）。
B is usually something sudden that does not last; if it lasts, switch to 〜間.
Can be used with the negative:見ている間に気づかなかった（didn't notice while watching）。

• Expresses that event B happens at some point during the period in which A is continuing.
• Mainly used when B is a short action/situation that ends quickly (鳴る、来る、起きる、入る…).
• When A is a lasting state (寝ている、留守にしている、会議中…), 〜間に is very natural.
• If B lasts throughout the whole period A, use 〜間 (without に).
fields.notes:
• N with a time-span meaning: 留守の間に／授業の間に／休憩の間に are very natural.
• In conversation, “この間” usually means “recently/the other day,” which is different from “間に”. Avoid confusing them.
• In written language, for coherence B can be placed before A: 電話が、映画を見ている間に、鳴った。
mistakes: Confusing 〜間 with 〜間に: if B lasts, do not use に. Incorrect example: 勉強している間に音楽を聞いた → better: 勉強している間、音楽を聞いた。
Using 〜うちに for a situation with no “change”: 映画を見ているうちに電話が鳴った → more natural with 〜間に.
The JLPT often asks you to choose between 〜間／〜間に／〜うちに based on whether clause B is a “point” or a “span”.

fields.meaning: Expresses that something has been completed early, as in examples ①②, or regret that it is impossible to return to a previous state, as in examples ③④.
examples: I'll get the report submitted tomorrow.
I've already finished reading the book I bought today.
I've forgotten that person's name.
Oh, your white clothes are going to get dirty!

fields.meaning: The sentence pattern ～てもいいです expresses permission or concession. ~てはいけません　expresses prohibition.
examples: I'm looking for a cheap room. It's fine if it's small.
Hana, you mustn't go to the river by yourself.
For the company entrance exam, a T-shirt is not acceptable.

Tom: "May I sit here?"
Woman: "Yes, go ahead."

fields.meaning: Expresses cause or reason. In many cases this pattern is used more than ~から／～ので　to state the cause or reason for certain feelings or emotions. After this pattern, besides words expressing emotion such as こまる、さびしい, etc., there are also words expressing the inability to carry out a
examples: I had a lot of work today, so it was tough.
I have no friends, so I'm lonely.
I was worried, so I couldn't sleep well.
Thank you for telling me.
I'm sorry I was late.

fields.connection: Vると/Vたら/Vば + いい（expectation, wish）
examples: "I hope your mother gets well soon."
"I hear tomorrow is the sports day. I hope it doesn't rain."
I hope I can get a scholarship this year.
It would be nice if our family could travel abroad next year.
fields.notes: Used both for advice/suggestion (～たらいいですよ) and for expectations/wishes

fields.meaning: Just when, right in the middle of | at the time~
examples: I'm about to go into a meeting now.
I'm just in the middle of explaining, so please wait a moment.
I've just finished applying a moment ago.
It started to rain just as I was leaving the house.
I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but please sign here.
I'm about to leave the house now.
fields.explain:
Add a time word: これから/ちょうど/たった今to make the meaning of about to/in the middle of/just clear.
In emails/at work: the opening phrase “お忙しいところ恐縮ですが…” is very polite.
V-たところ: often states a discovery/result right after an experience:調べ たところ、～が分かった。
V-るところ is rarely used with lasting actions; it suits the moment of starting.

- “ところ” marks the point/stage (time point) of an action: before it starts (V-る), while it is happening (V-ている), just after it ends (V-た).
- V-たところ emphasizes “just now” more than たばかり (it feels more immediate). V-ているところ emphasizes the immediacy of “right in the middle of”.
- With particles:
- ところに/へ: just when (something comes/goes) “arrived just as … was …”.
- ところを: even though (in a state), another action has an effect; also used in keigo “お忙しいところを…” (apologizing/thanking).
- ところで: has the conjunction meaning “by the way” (not the time aspect of V); be careful to distinguish it.
fields.notes:
- The pattern “V-たところ、～” is often used in reports/conclusions: “After doing V, (I) found out/realized…”. This is a structure that states the result of a short investigation/test.
- “ところを” goes with verbs of apologizing/thanking: お忙しいところを申し訳ありません／ありがとうございます。
- Note the ambiguity of V-るところ: add a time adverb “今から/これから/ちょうど” to make it clear it means “about to”.
mistakes: Confusing V-たところ with たばかり: the JLPT often tests the “immediate” nuance of たところ.
Mixing up ところで (conjunction) with ところ＋particle: their functions are completely different.
Using V-るところ for a lasting action (×明日旅行に行くところだ) → better to use 前/直前/行くところ “right when about to go” with the context “今/これから”.
Forgetting the correct particle: 来たところに電話が… / 邪魔しているところをすみません。

examples: Yesterday, Mr. Takagi said he would come at 8 tomorrow. But he hasn't come yet.
The TV news said there was an earthquake in Chiba early this morning.
Yesterday's weather forecast said the rain would probably continue for a while.
"I heard there's a TV (program) next week. Is that true?"
My mother's letter said that last week's festival was very lively and fun.

Note:
●　「　」があるときは、「　　」の中はていねい体でもよい
when there is 「　　」, the polite form can also be used inside 「　　」。
1.高木さんはきのう、「あした８時に来ます」と言いました。

examples: For my health, I've decided not to eat after 9 p.m.
I want to save money, so I decided not to eat out.
This month, I make a point of not wasting money.
I'm busy, so I'll decide not to go on the weekend trip.
Today I decided not to buy any sweet drinks.
fields.explain:
Used for personal decisions; emphasizes the speaker's volition/control.
To be polite to the listener: 〜ことにしました（I have decided…）.
Can go with a reason/motive before or after: 〜ので／〜ために + ないことにする.
In a promise to oneself: よし、今日は文句を言わ ないことにする ！

• Expresses a subjective decision by the speaker: “decide not to do V”.
• The form 〜ことにした emphasizes the point in time when the decision was made in the past; 〜ことにしている emphasizes a present habit/rule.
• Can be used for a temporary decision (today) or a long-term one (from now on) depending on context.
• Different from 〜ないことになる: 〜ないことにする means deciding oneself; 〜ないことになる means it is decided by circumstances/rules.
fields.notes:
• This negative form often goes with consumption/health/bad habit behaviors: 飲まない・食べない・買わない・行かない・言わない.
• To emphasize that it is temporary: 今日は〜しないことにする; long-term: これからは〜しないことにする.
• In conversation, it can be used as a “reminder to oneself,” with a nuance of determination.
mistakes: Confusing it with 〜ないことになる: exam questions often require distinguishing who makes the decision. “会社の方針で飲まないことになった”（because of the company) ≠ “自分で飲まないことにした”.
Use 〜ことにした when telling about a past decision; use 〜ことにする when declaring/setting a rule in the present.
Wrong tense: attaching だ after ことにする is incorrect. There is no “〜ないことにするだ”.
Overusing it with non-volitional behavior: “雨を見ないことにする” is meaningless; use it only for behavior that can be controlled.

examples: You shouldn't push yourself too hard today.
You'd better not tell the department manager about that.
It's better not to go out alone at night.
You shouldn't take that medicine on an empty stomach.
It's better not to ask very personal questions when meeting someone for the first time.
The rain is heavy, so I think you'd better not go today.
fields.explain:
Polite: ～ないほうがいいです; Neutral: ～ないほうがいいよ; Softened: ～ないほうがいいと思います。
Used when the listener is free to decide; avoid using it with superiors (switch to ～てはいかがですか/おすすめしません).
When comparing two options, both can be stated:行くより行か ないほうがいい。
Often accompanied by a reason: ～から/ので/ほうがいい。
Not used for actions that have already happened (for regret, use ～ないほうがよかった).

• Advice/suggestion: “You shouldn't do …” based on experience, common sense, or the speaker's opinion.
• Softer nuance than a command; often used when giving personal advice, about health care or safety.
• Shows a choice: between two possibilities, the option of “not doing” is better.
• Not used for an organization's absolute prohibitions (then use ～てはいけない/禁止).
• Often accompanied by ですよ/と思います/かもしれません to reduce directness.
• Compared with ～べきではない: weaker, less moralizing/judgmental; leans toward practical advice.
fields.notes:
• Writing: both ほう and 方 are seen; in formal written language 方 is usually used.
• To be even more polite: ～ないほうがよろしいかと思います。
• Add grounds from experience: ～ないほうがいいですよ、前に失敗しましたから。
• In conversation, drop です to sound casual: ～ないほうがいいよ。
mistakes: Wrong form: using 辞書形 instead of ない形. Correct: 行かないほうがいい (not 行くほうがいい when you mean “should not”).
Confusing it with absolute prohibition: ～てはいけない is stronger and more rule-like.
Not distinguishing regret: if it already happened, use ～ないほうがよかった.
Irregular verbs: する→しないほうがいい；来る→来ない（こない）ほうがいい。
Rude when said to a superior/customer: change it into an indirect suggestion to be polite.

Better not to do it (less bad)

fields.connection: Vなければいけない → Vなきゃいけない（contraction; 急がなきゃ）
examples: I have to go to bed soon.
The deadline's here, so I've got to hurry.
I have to get up early tomorrow.
Do I have to eat that much?
I have to go pick up my child.
Looks like it's going to rain. I've got to bring the laundry in.
fields.explain:
Very colloquial; used in conversation, chat, and quick notes. Avoid it in formal documents.
The ending is often omitted when the context is clear: もう出かけ なきゃ。High sense of urgency.
Combines well with ちょっと／やっぱ／もう／そろそろ to sound natural: もう行かなきゃ。

• Expresses the meaning “must/have to” in a casual way, in everyday conversation.
• Origin: なきゃ＝なければ (contraction) → “If (you) don't …, it's not OK” → implies having to do it.
• Softer nuance than ～なければならない; the casual equivalent of ～ないといけない/～なくてはいけない.
fields.notes:
• Sound changes in conversation: ～なきゃ → ～なきゃぁ／～なきゃね to soften.
• The information focus is usually placed before なきゃ for emphasis: 絶対今日中に終わらせなきゃ。
• Negating the obligation uses a different structure: 行かなくてもいい／行かなくてはならないの否定ではない.
mistakes: Confusing it with the prohibition ～てはいけない: the meaning is completely different.
Using it in formal written language (essays/applications): change it to ～なければならない／～ないといけません.
Writing the original form incorrectly: なきゃ＝なければ, なくちゃ＝なくては; avoid the combination “なきゃては”.
Omitting the ending on an exam: もう出かけなきゃ… → if it is not conversation, write it out in full to avoid losing points.

rows: <ruby>守<rt>まも</rt></ruby>らなければならない
<ruby>勉強<rt>べんきょう</rt></ruby>しなくちゃ

examples: I have to get up early tomorrow.
I have to submit it by the deadline.
It has to be quiet here, so make your calls outside.
I've got to go now!
I have to get in touch (with them).
fields.explain:
Formality: spoken language. In written language/formal situations, prefer ～なくてはいけない／～なければならない.
Person: usually I/we; rarely used to directly order the listener (it sounds harsh). For gentle advice: ～ほうがいい/～たほうがいい.
Negating the obligation: use ～ なくてもいい (no need to), not the negative of いけない.
Polite: ～なくちゃ いけません can be used, but it mixes colloquial and polite; normally use ～なくてはいけません.

• Main meaning: obligation/requirement at a casual level: “have to ...”, “definitely have to ...”.
• Nuance: softer than ～なければならない; has the feel of “reminding oneself”, “group rules”, or “strong advice” in conversation.
• Source of the obligation: can be oneself, a schedule, not-very-formal rules, the family/friend context.
• Omission of いけない: when the speaker is in a hurry/noting something to do, they just say ～なくちゃ／～なきゃ.
fields.notes:
• Basis: ～なくちゃ is a contraction of ～なくては. “ちゃ” comes from “ては” → “ちゃ”.
• ～ないと (いけない/だめ) is very common; when the latter part is omitted, the context supplies the meaning “have to”.
• With Aい/N/na: the meaning “need to (be in a state) ...” is often used when describing conditions to be met: 安くなくちゃいけない (it has to be cheap).
• In polite communication with customers/partners, avoid ～なくちゃ; choose ～なくてはいけません.
mistakes: Forgetting “で” before なくちゃいけない with N/na: ×静かなくちゃいけない → 〇静かでなくちゃいけない.
Using it as a direct command to a superior: sounds rude. Switch to ～てください or ～ていただけますか.
Confusing it with negating the obligation using いけない: ×行かなくちゃいけなくない → 〇行かなくてもいい.
Formal writing: avoid ～なくちゃ in reports/written exams; use ～なくてはいけない／～なければならない.

fields.meaning: The sentence pattern ～なくてもいいですexpresses lack of necessity or concession. ～なければなりませんexpresses necessity, an obligation to do something.
examples: Is there a good hotel? It doesn't have to be close to the station.
Mom, do we have a box? It doesn't have to be sturdy.
I have to write a reply to the email.
The signature here must be yours.

Doctor: "You don't need to take the medicine anymore."
Patient: "Really? Oh, what a relief."

fields.meaning: Turns a verb into a noun.
examples: I like reading books.
Living alone is lonely, but it's nice because you're free.
I'm good at reading texts, but I'm bad at writing.
"Do you know that Mr. Chin is getting married next month?"
fields.notes:
Note:
●次のような文では、「こと」しか使えない。
In sentences like the following, only 「こと」 can be used
1.  わたしの趣味は映画を見ることです。
My hobby is watching movies
2.  わたしが日本へ来た目的は、日本語の勉強をすることです。
My purpose in coming to Japan is to study Japanese.

examples: During summer vacation, I went to my grandparents' house.
I finished the laundry while my child was sleeping.
A burglar broke in while I was away.
During the meeting, the phone rang only once.
While I was a student, I took part in an exchange program abroad.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes a “point” within a span: used for a single event that cuts into a lasting period.
Neutral formality: works well in both spoken and written language; on signs, ～中/～の際 are often used instead depending on context.
Leans toward a lasting background state: before ～の間に there is usually a noun expressing a time span that lasts.

• “While/during”: expresses an action/event that happens at some point within the stated time period.
• Time coverage: ～間に leans toward “a point/a few times within the span,” unlike ～間, which emphasizes “throughout, in parallel”.
• Natural combinations: time nouns (休み、会議、授業、在学) or Vている to express a lasting state.
Core difference: A間、B (B takes place throughout A). A間に、B (B happens once/a few times during A).
fields.notes:
• Vている + 間に is more natural than Vる + 間に with verbs of duration: 彼がいる間に vs 彼がいている間に (both are seen, but Vている makes the state clear).
• Nouns expressing states: 留守/在学/勤務/出張 など go very well with ～の間に.
• “この間” also means “recently”; but “この間に” emphasizes a specific period that has just passed.
mistakes: Mixing up 間 and 間に: a lasting event must use 間, a point event uses 間に.
Using Vる + 間に with a punctual verb sounds awkward: ×帰る間に 盗まれた → ○帰っている間に? In practice, use ～うちに/～とちゅうで depending on the meaning.
Forgetting 「の」 after a noun: ×夏休み間に → ○夏休みの間に.

(I) have a stomachache / my eyes are tired / I have a fever.
